*Generated by research-copilot overnight, 2026-05-18.*

# Feedback on your overnight ideas

You wrote a clean reformulation of the doc-grounded meta-harness problem
and gave per-proposal commentary. This document responds in kind. I tried
to be a useful interlocutor — agreeing where I agreed, pushing back where
I think your reasoning has a soft spot, and surfacing the missing pieces I
think the proposal needs before it can convince an advisor.

The conclusion up front:

- **Your "study-the-textbook" framing is the right north star.** It is
  also the framing most directly underdeveloped in the four baselines we
  reviewed. Sharpening it is the highest-leverage thing you can do this
  week.
- **The crisp form of the claim is *not* "the meta-harness reads the
  docs" — it's "the meta-harness emits a re-usable, harness-shaped
  artifact distilled from the docs, before any task is attempted."** That
  artifact is what makes "studying" different from "open-book RAG." It is
  also what makes the contribution falsifiable.
- **N4 (doc-bootstrapped seed) is the operational backbone of this
  framing.** N2 (bipartite) is the structural commitment that makes the
  artifact maintainable across iterations. N3 is a clean
  attribution-side novelty. N6 is the caching/promotion mechanism that
  closes the loop. **My recommendation is N4 ⊕ N2 as the spine, N3 and
  N6 as the supporting studies.** Skip N1 for now (it's subsumed under
  the artifact format).

The rest of this document spells out the reasoning.

---

## 1. The strongest framing of your core idea

Your re-statement (paraphrased): humans access docs at runtime, but
humans who already studied the docs *use* runtime access better. A new
employee who has skimmed the manual is faster at re-finding things than
one who hasn't. The LLM analogue can't be fine-tuning (too expensive on
frontier models), so the alternative is to *force a deliberate study
pass* over the docs by the meta-harness, with **note-writing as the
mechanism that distinguishes study from no-op reading**.

This is a real research question. Let me push on it.

### 1a. Why "study" is genuinely different from RAG

You already half-articulated this — let me make the distinction sharper,
because it's the load-bearing claim:

- **RAG is *reactive*.** A query arrives; the system retrieves what
  the query asks for. The selection function is `f: query → sections`.
  Reactive retrieval is bounded by query quality.
- **Study is *proactive*.** Before any query, the agent has decided
  what's *worth knowing*. The agent has imposed a structure on the
  material (what's a "schema entity", what's a "deprecation warning",
  which workflows are common). Selection during retrieval becomes
  `f: query → studied-structure → sections`, where the studied
  structure mediates and can promote, prune, or reframe the raw
  retrieval.

The bitter-lesson concern you flagged in N4 deserves a direct counter on
this point. Bitter lesson says general methods that scale with compute
eventually win over hand-engineered ones. But the bitter lesson assumes
**the compute can be cheaply scaled at inference time**. Our setting is
the opposite: each "evaluation" of a harness involves running the
harness end-to-end on a task suite. **The expensive thing is not
training the agent's mind — it's evaluating proposed harnesses**. In
this regime, anything that improves the *prior* over what a good harness
looks like (a strong seed, a structured doc index, a known taxonomy of
failures) is a multiplier on every subsequent evaluation. That's why
NAS papers spend a huge fraction of their compute on warm-starting from
strong priors. Same shape of problem.

So: yes, in the limit, "infinite compute + grep" wins. But the limit is
2-3 orders of magnitude away. The contribution lives in that gap.

### 1b. The note-writing artifact is the *whole* contribution

Here's where I want to push back on your draft slightly. Re-read your
own §32:

> Proposal: maybe we can force the meta-agent to traverse the entire
> documentation, read every file and write notes for itself ... and then
> hierarchically coalesce these notes into global understanding which
> might take the material form of a coding agent-optimized map ...

You called this "the proposal." I want to argue that it *is* the
contribution. Let me be specific about what's load-bearing:

1. **Traversal coverage** — the meta-agent must touch every doc file (or
   at least every doc *section* under some declared coverage rule). This
   is what distinguishes the system from RAG-on-demand. Falsifiable: log
   coverage; ablate coverage threshold.

2. **Persistent notes per section** — each section produces a
   structured artifact (not just a context-window read that evaporates).
   The structure is what makes the notes useful to a later harness.
   Falsifiable: ablate by replacing structured notes with raw text
   excerpts of equal token count.

3. **Hierarchical coalescing** — local section notes feed into
   higher-level summaries. This is where the *"coding-agent-optimized
   map"* lives. Falsifiable: ablate by replacing coalesced map with
   flat concatenation of section notes.

4. **The artifact is what the harness sees at runtime** — not the raw
   docs. The harness retrieves *over the studied map*, not over the
   bare doc tree. Falsifiable: ablate by letting the harness see only
   the raw docs, only the map, or both.

That ablation lattice (2×3×2 = 12, prune to ~6 meaningful) is the
empirical backbone of the paper. None of MH/MCE/AHE/SF have anything
equivalent because none of them produce a doc-shaped artifact that the
runtime harness consumes.

### 1c. The risk you didn't name

The risk that needs to be acknowledged in any honest writeup: if frontier
LLMs are already implicitly "studied" on most public scientific docs
(they were trained on the manuals), the study pass might be a no-op for
in-distribution tools and only pay off on **out-of-distribution or
private docs** (versions newer than the training cutoff, internal lab
codebases, proprietary tools).

This is actually a *strength* of the framing if you reframe it as: "the
contribution is most valuable exactly where you can't fine-tune and can't
rely on training data" — i.e., the realistic deployment setting. But it
needs to be stated. Otherwise an adversarial reviewer will ask "did you
just rediscover what the base model already knows?"

**Concrete empirical hook:** include at least one tool whose docs
substantially post-date the LLM's training cutoff, or one tool whose docs
are private to a project. GEOS is borderline (open-source but
specialized); FEniCS/MOOSE are similar. The cleanest version of this
test is a doc *diff* — take a GEOS version newer than the model knows,
and check whether the studied-notes condition handles new constructs
better than baseline RAG.

## 2. Per-proposal feedback (responding to your §35-§54)

### N2 (bipartite component↔section graph) — strongly agree, with a wrinkle

You said: "this is something I briefly explored as an early
implementation: can we take advantage of subagents?" — I want to
disentangle two claims that I think are getting bundled together in your
mind:

- **Claim A**: N2 is structurally valuable (the bipartite graph is the
  right abstraction).
- **Claim B**: Subagent orchestration is the right *implementation* of
  N2.

Claim A is clean and I agree. The bipartite graph gives you a
*type-checked symmetry* between the harness and the docs: every
component declares which sections it grounds in; every section is either
cited (live) or uncited (dead). This is what makes the meta-harness's
edits accountable.

Claim B is a separate question. **Subagent orchestration is one way to
maintain the graph but not the only way**, and the prior negative result
you mentioned is a real signal worth respecting. Let me argue for a
middle path:

- The graph itself is structured data (nodes, edges, citations).
  Maintaining it does not *require* subagents.
- Subagents are useful when (i) a sub-task has a bounded scope, (ii) it
  benefits from context isolation (e.g., reading a single doc section
  without polluting context), (iii) parallelization wins on wall-clock.
- For documentation **traversal** (read 200 doc files, write 200 sets
  of notes), subagents are a clean fit: bounded scope, context
  isolation, parallel.
- For graph **maintenance** (edits, consistency checks, dead-section
  detection), subagents are a worse fit: needs global state, mostly
  serial, small per-step compute.

**Recommendation**: use subagents only for the parallel-and-isolated
parts of N2 (initial traversal, batch consistency checks). Use a single
controller process to maintain the graph proper. That avoids the prior
performance failure while keeping the part of subagent orchestration
that actually helps.

There's a small concrete win here too: subagents are how you get a
*linear* token cost on traversal (each subagent reads one section,
~5-50K tokens) rather than a quadratic one (single agent's context grows
as it reads more). This was the original argument and it's still right.

### N3 (doc-anchored failure attribution) — agree, can be smaller

You said this "potentially interesting, probably worth testing." Agree.
My one structural note: N3 stands or falls on whether
**doc-anchored 3-way classification actually beats AHE's free-form
attribution**. AHE's number (11.8% precision on regression prediction)
is the right baseline to beat.

The relevant operationalization: collect a corpus of regressions during a
real run, hand-label each one as (a/b/c) per N3, then ask the agent to
predict (a/b/c) given the trajectory + doc index. Compare to AHE's free-
form prediction. This is a clean, small, falsifiable study that can fit
in a 1-page appendix.

This could even be done *independently* of the meta-harness training
loop — just collect AHE-style trajectories from any agent on GEOS, label
them, run the classification eval. **Cheap and high-information.** Worth
prioritizing.

### N4 (doc-bootstrapped seed harness) — strongly agree, this is the spine

You correctly identified the bitter-lesson tension here. I gave my
counter in §1a above (the expensive thing is harness evaluation, so
priors matter disproportionately).

Adding two operational notes:

1. **The seed is itself a "study artifact."** This is the right way to
   unify N4 with your study-the-docs framing. The seed harness is
   literally the output of the study pass — entrypoints, primary
   objects, top-level workflows extracted from doc structural metadata.
   So "doc-bootstrapped seed" and "study artifact" are the same
   thing viewed from two angles.

2. **The ablation should isolate "doc-bootstrapped seed alone" vs
   "doc-bootstrapped seed + iterative refinement."** If (a) alone is
   already strong, then the meta-harness's iterative loop is doing less
   work than people thought. That's an interesting finding either way.

### N6 (doc-utility–weighted search budget) — agree, but reframe

You correctly read this as "caching logic — promote frequently-accessed
info to a higher level." That's exactly right.

The reframing I'd suggest: **don't put N6 in the proposal as a separate
research thread.** Bundle it inside N2 as the *update rule* for the
bipartite graph — sections cited by harnesses that improve get
strengthened; sections that fire alongside regressions get demoted. That
way N6 becomes the dynamics, not a separate proposal.

This is a strict simplification of the design (fewer numbered ideas,
fewer paragraphs to read) and a sharper claim ("the graph has explicit
update rules learned from utility, not just static citation").

### Items I'd cut for this paper

- **N1 (typed multi-index)** — your study-the-docs framing already
  produces a typed map. The typed multi-index is a *byproduct*, not a
  contribution. Don't double-count.
- **N7 (symmetric doc-consultation traces)** — overlaps heavily with N2
  if N2 is properly logged. Cut for clarity; mention in limitations as
  "we instrument doc consultation but don't yet make it a separate
  observability channel."
- **N8 (negative knowledge as constraints)** — interesting, but it's a
  paper of its own. Park.
- **N9 (doc-diff)** — explicitly long-horizon. Park.
- **N5 (doc-as-soft-oracle)** — I'd actually keep this if budget
  permits, because it gives you a cheap proxy metric independent of
  expensive ground-truth evaluation. But if you have to cut, this is
  the next thing to cut after N1/N7.

## 3. The proposal shape I'd commit to

Re-reading the design memo (`docs/2026-05-14_doc-grounded-meta-harness-
proposals.md`) with your overnight comments in mind, here's what I think
the cleanest paper looks like:

**Title (working):** *Study-then-Harness: Documentation-Grounded
Meta-Harness Construction via Pre-Task Doc Distillation*

**One-sentence claim:** Forcing the meta-harness to *study* the
documentation (read everything, write structured notes, coalesce
hierarchically) before constructing the runtime harness produces a
better, more interpretable, more maintainable harness than letting the
meta-harness consult docs only on-demand.

**Three pieces of empirical evidence the paper needs:**

1. **Sanity**: the studied artifact alone, used as a static prompt
   prefix for the harness, beats a flat-doc-RAG baseline on the eval
   tasks. (Cheap.)
2. **Symmetry**: a meta-harness that *itself* operates over the studied
   artifact (rather than the raw docs) makes better edits to the
   harness than one operating over raw docs. (Medium.)
3. **Attribution**: when regressions occur, doc-anchored 3-way
   classification (N3) predicts the cause better than free-form AHE
   attribution. (Independent, cheap-ish.)

**The ablation lattice you actually run:**
- A0 = vanilla CC, no docs
- A1 = vanilla CC + flat docs in FS (MH-style)
- A2 = vanilla CC + RAG over docs (SF-flavored)
- A3 = vanilla CC + **studied artifact** (no raw docs)
- A4 = vanilla CC + **studied artifact + raw docs both available**
- A5 = meta-harness iterating with **studied artifact as substrate**
  vs **raw docs as substrate** (the core experiment)

A0–A4 are static evals — fast. A5 is the headline meta-harness training
loop.

## 4. Things that are unresolved (questions for you)

1. **Tool choice.** GEOS is what we have working infra for. FEniCS or
   MOOSE for cross-tool transfer is a nice-to-have, not core. Are you
   committed to a multi-tool story for Paper 2, or willing to ship a
   single-tool depth paper with cross-tool as future work?
2. **Coding-agent vs staged-pipeline meta-harness.** Design memo §7
   leans staged. Your overnight write-up is agnostic. I lean staged for
   the same reasons (explicit places to plug structured artifacts in).
   Confirm?
3. **Proposer model.** DSv4-flash is fine for the harness (cheap). For
   the *meta-harness proposer* the paper might want a stronger model
   (Gemini 3 Flash? Opus 4.6?), because the meta-harness is the loop
   we're paying compute for. Are you OK letting cost-per-iteration
   creep up at the meta level?
4. **Evaluation surface.** Input-file fidelity (treesim) is what we
   have. Do we want to add end-to-end simulation success (slower but
   more meaningful) for at least a held-out subset?

## 5. Suggested search queries for your literature pass

You asked for search terms to feed into Asta / Semantic Scholar / Google
Scholar / your AI deep-research tool of choice. Here's a categorized
list, ordered by what I think will be highest-signal first.

### 5a. The "LLMs reading to learn" branch

This is the closest existing research branch to what you're proposing.
Most relevant query stems:

- `"pre-task" OR "pre-reading" documentation LLM agent`
- `agent "study phase" documentation distillation`
- `LLM "note taking" documentation knowledge artifact`
- `"book-as-knowledge-graph" OR "manual-to-structure" LLM`
- `agent "warmup" "domain adaptation" without fine-tuning`
- `RAG vs "context distillation" knowledge artifact`
- `"hierarchical summarization" technical documentation LLM`
- `"long-document study" pre-task agent preparation`
- `LLM "self-supervised note taking"`
- `"reading to learn" language model agent`

### 5b. Closest adjacent areas worth surveying

- **Continuous pre-training on docs** — `"continued pretraining" "domain
  adaptation" technical manual` (related, but the "we can't fine-tune"
  framing is exactly the differentiation).
- **Skill libraries / capability mining** — `"skill library" LLM agent
  documentation` (SkillFoundry sits here).
- **Memory-augmented agents** — `"long-term memory" LLM agent "knowledge
  consolidation"` (MemP, ExpeL — related but trajectory-based, not doc-
  based).
- **Programming-by-doc / API understanding** — `"API documentation"
  "code generation" LLM "structured representation"` (lots here, mostly
  for general programming; less for scientific tools).
- **Hierarchical retrieval** — `"hierarchical RAG" OR "tree-of-
  retrieval" structured documents`.
- **Educational analogy** — `"open-book exam" LLM evaluation` (you
  flagged this analogy; there's some real lit here).

### 5c. Concept-anchor queries (search for these specific named systems)

These named systems are the most-likely-to-exist prior art. Search them
directly; if they exist, read them:

- `"DocAgent"`, `"DocStudy"`, `"StudyAgent"`, `"PreparedAgent"` —
  guesses at plausible existing system names
- `"meta-learning" "documentation" LLM`
- `"agent priming" knowledge base`
- `"tool documentation" "agent" structured representation`
- `Toolformer` / `ToolLLM` / `Gorilla` — well-known
  function-from-docs work; cite as related, not core
- `KNOWAGENT` / `AgentVerse` / `Voyager` — agent skill induction work
- `Reflexion` / `Self-Refine` — trajectory-based memory, contrast
- `ExpeL` / `MemP` / `MemGPT` — memory baselines you already know
- `ProAgent`, `SciAgent`, `BiomedAgent` — domain-grounded agent papers

### 5d. Negative-result hunting (be honest)

- `"domain knowledge injection" hurt OR negative OR baseline`
  (MoSciBench is here; there's probably more)
- `"context distillation" failure`
- `"hierarchical summarization" information loss`
- `RAG outperforms fine-tuning OR pre-training`

### 5e. Asta / deep research–specific framing

For Asta or any "deep research" tool that benefits from question-shaped
prompts (rather than keyword queries), try:

- "What is the strongest published result for forcing an LLM agent to
  pre-read documentation before task execution, and how does it compare
  to retrieval-only baselines?"
- "Are there published LLM-agent systems that produce a persistent,
  hierarchical artifact distilled from technical documentation before
  any task is attempted?"
- "What is the prior art for using a meta-controller (agent that
  builds agents) to study documentation, separate from in-the-loop
  RAG?"
- "How do scientific-software agents (BioMni, SpatialAgent, GeoAgent
  variants) handle documentation that wasn't in the model's training
  data?"
- "What's the closest analogue in NAS literature to bootstrapping the
  search from a doc-derived prior?"

### 5f. Concrete advisor-ready references to cite no matter what

Read past these even if other searches don't find better:

- Meta-Harness (Lee et al. 2026) — LN-003
- AHE (Lin et al. 2026) — `meta_harness_reading/observability_driven_evolution.md`
- MCE (Ye et al. 2026) — `meta_harness_reading/meta_context_engineering.md`
- SkillFoundry (Shen et al. 2026) — LN-004 (the one you definitely read carefully)

Newly worth a deep skim:

## 7. Bottom-line recommendations

If you have only 10 minutes in the morning, read this:

1. **Commit to "study artifact" as the contribution.** Stop describing
   the paper as "doc-grounded meta-harness." Start describing it as
   "the meta-harness produces a *studied artifact* before any task
   runs; everything downstream consumes that artifact." Sharper, easier
   to falsify, less defensible-to-reviewers ambiguity.
2. **N4 ⊕ N2 is the spine.** Bootstrap from doc-derived structure (N4),
   maintain it as a bipartite graph that explicitly types
   harness↔doc-section relationships (N2). N6 becomes the update
   dynamics inside N2.
3. **N3 is independent and cheap.** Run it. It can ship as a paper
   appendix or as a standalone arxiv contribution if Paper 2 takes
   longer.
4. **Acknowledge the in-distribution risk.** State it. Design at least
   one experiment around a post-cutoff or private tool to neutralize
   it.
5. **Read SkillFoundry's actual code, not the GPT summary.** LN-004
   already flags this. The staged-pipeline detail is what determines
   how cleanly your novelties slot in.

That's the proposal sharpened. The advisor-ready version is in the
companion document.
